…, since the Son of God works everywhere, it must be that his flesh is present everywhere.* Answer. In this place, Osiander rehashes and casts back at us the first argument of the Apollinarian heretics, who attributed Deity to the flesh of Christ, just as a soul is attributed to a body. Furthermore, the very likeness used by Osiander overturns the omnipresence of the flesh of Christ. For just as a soul, even though hypostatically united to a body, does not exercise all its operations through the body, such as meditating, reasoning, and the like: so too the Deity of Christ does not perfect all its actions through his humanity, even after the union. Therefore, it does not conclude that it is present everywhere.

 Page 28. *The humanity assumed by Christ is one person with his own Deity, and is hypostatically united with it. Therefore, wherever the Deity of Christ is, there also is his flesh or humanity.* Answer. First, this man formerly took the presence of Christ in the Lord’s Supper not from the hypostatic union, but from these words of Christ: "This is my body." Next, recognizing that this protection of his is weak, he now abandons it, and turns himself toward the hypostatic union.

Noailles was terrified all the more by the Council of Embrun and by the King's authority in upholding its acts. In the year 1727, many bishops had gathered at Embrun to overthrow the monstrous errors which were being scattered here and there by the schismatics, and to compose the disturbances incited by the same. There were, furthermore, two principal acts: the condemnation of Father Courrayer of the monastery of Sainte-Geneviève, along with his book against the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist—who, intending to carry out the system of Dupin , crossed over into England and exalted himself there with other writings on the ordinations of Anglican bishops—and the other, the sentence passed on September 20th against Soanen, Bishop of Senez. A certain pastoral instruction had appeared under his name, teeming with infamous errors of every kind, and in which, to the extent that the work of Quesnel was commended, the Bull condemning it was held up as worthy of every execration. This instruction was condemned

Soanen, having initially prevaricated, and thirteen bishops having been named before whom he might plead his case, and against whom he himself had no objections to raise, finally set out for Embrun, not without a profane retinue, which was not unarmed.
